problem: Frontier-based exploration for mapless object-goal navigation uses random or nearest-frontier ordering, which causes inefficient back-and-forth movement. Learning-based ordering (TSP/RL) depends on specific datasets and generalizes poorly.
motivation: Choosing the frontier visiting order strongly affects exploration efficiency in complex environments. LLMs have commonsense knowledge about where objects are found, and the authors argue LLMs judge relative value between frontiers better than absolute value, so ranking should be more reliable than scoring.
key_idea: Use an LLM as a ranking model over frontiers/view directions given detected objects, convert ranks to reciprocal-rank vectors (optionally weighted by distance) and fuse them over views to choose the next frontier subgoal.
insight: The only evidence is a small proof-of-concept comparison: LLM-ranked frontier selection gives higher SPL than random frontier selection in all three HM3D scenes (e.g. 0.426 vs 0.366 in scene 800), with gains shrinking to 0.335 vs 0.324 in scene 802. Reciprocal rank vectors offer a simple way to fuse independent LLM rankings across views and queries. There is no deeper ablation, so why it works is only argued, not shown.
method: Frontier ranking formulation: candidate frontiers F={f_i} are ranked by the LLM for the target object; the score is S_i = w_i / r_i, with w_i a monotonically decreasing function of distance, and the best frontier is argmax S.
Reciprocal Rank Feature fusion: each LLM ranking is a reciprocal-rank vector; independent rankings from new viewpoints are fused by adding vectors, giving a scalar frontier score map (called QOM).
Perception: robot captures 8 views (45° steps); closed-vocabulary Mask R-CNN detects objects, which are turned into text.

View-to-prompt design: the LLM first classifies the room category for each view from detected objects, then picks the likely room for the target, then ranks the 8 directional views by likelihood of containing the target; the top direction is chosen.
Subgoal selection: a random frontier within the top-ranked direction becomes the subgoal, and unselected directions that contain frontiers are kept for later decisions.
Motion planning: occupancy grid map, frontier detection, A* path planning, and an idealized bumper sensor for collisions; replan after each arrival until the target is detected.

setting.backbone: Google Gemini (frozen, version unspecified) + Mask R-CNN (closed-vocabulary detector)
setting.observation: 8-direction RGB views at each viewpoint (plus occupancy grid map)
setting.action_space: frontier subgoals moved to via A* on an occupancy grid
setting.privileged: none stated (idealized bumper sensor for collision avoidance)

numbers_note: Only SPL on three self-defined HM3D MINIVAL scenes; no SR, and no comparison with published ObjectNav methods. Text and table disagree on the random-frontier SPL for scene 801 (0.328 vs 0.338).
results: LGR beats the random-frontier ablation in SPL in all three scenes: 0.426 vs 0.366, 0.359 vs 0.338 (text says 0.328), and 0.335 vs 0.324. These are relative gains of about 16.4%, 6.2% and 3.4%. Authors call it proof-of-concept.
limitations: Very small evaluation: three scenes, SPL only, compared only to a random-frontier baseline, with no standard benchmark or strong baselines.
Closed-vocabulary detector, random frontier within the chosen direction, and an idealized bumper sensor; the frontier-list update rule is left as future work and LLMs cannot rank long frontier lists.
